title: Relative Quantitative Analysis of Site-Specific N-Linked Glycosylation in Hyperglycosylated In-terferon-β via Mass Spectrometry
projectDescription: Glycosylation is a critical determinant of the efficacy, stability, and pharmacological behavior of therapeutic proteins. R27T, an engineered variant of interferon-β1a, contains two N-glycosylation sites (Asn25 and Asn80), increasing its structural complexity and analytical requirements. In this study, we performed comprehensive total and site-specific glycan profiling of R27T using complementary analytical approaches. For total glycan analysis, the released N-glycans were fluorescently labeled with procainamide, providing enhanced sensitivity and broader glycan coverage compared with conventional 2-aminobenzamide labeling. Site-specific glycan profiling was performed by LC–MS/MS–based peptide mapping. Protease digestion conditions were optimized to improve recovery of site-specific glycopeptides, with chymotryp-sin identified as the most effective enzyme for resolving glycopeptides from individual glyco-sylation sites. Total glycan distributions reconstructed from peptide-mapping data were com-pared with fluorescence-based glycan profiling, showing that total and site-specific glycan data can be effectively combined. Minor discrepancies were observed depending on glycan struc-ture, mainly due to differences in ionization efficiency. Distinct glycan distributions were iden-tified between the two N-glycosylation sites of R27T. Molecular modeling further suggested that the additional glycan at Asn25 may enhance structural stability and receptor-binding affini-ty. These results demonstrate an integrative strategy for accurate glycan characterization in mul-ti-site glycoproteins relevant to biotherapeutic development.
dataProcessingProtocol: N-linked Glycan Profiling Data analysis was performed using Byos software (version 5.3.44; Protein Metrics Inc.). Peptide Mapping Data processing was performed using the “N-glycan 309 mammalian no sodium” database from Protein Metrics. Glycoprotein-Receptor Complex Modeling with AlphaFold3  To investigate the structural and functional impact of the R27T-induced glycosylation site, two distinct models of the human IFN-β1 signaling complex were generated using AlphaFold3 (AF3). (41) Both models included the full-length extracellular domains of IFNAR1 (UniProt: P17181) and IFNAR2 (UniProt: P48551) receptors. The first model (Model 1, Control) consisted of wild-type IFN-β1 (N80-glycosylated) complexed with IFNAR1/IFNAR2.The second model (Model 2, R27T Variant) consisted of the engineered R27T variant (N25/N80-glycosylated) complexed with IFNAR1/IFNAR2. Structural modeling required precise specification of N-linked glycans, achieved by employing a hybrid input syntax combining Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) codes with explicit “bondedAtomPairs” (BAP) definitions within the AF3 JSON input. (42) This advanced protocol ensures stereochemically, conformationally accurate models, as standard linear input formats can introduce ambiguities. The specific N-glycan structures modeled at each site were based on the most abundant glycoforms identified in our MS data. For the N80 site (present in both models), the A2G2FS1 glycan was modelled. For the N25 site (present only in Model 2), the highly complex A4G4FS2 + 1LacNAc glycan was modeled. The BAP syntax defines the precise covalent glycosidic linkages between monosaccharide units. For example, to link the first N-acetylglucosamine (NAG, CCD code) to the asparagine (Asn) residue, a bond was defined between the Asn Nδ2 atom and the NAG C1 atom. Subsequent linkages (e.g., the β(1,4) linkage between the first and second NAG residues) were defined by specifying a bond between the O4 atom of the first NAG and the C1 atom of the second NAG, following the protocol described by Huang et al. (2025). This protocol-driven approach ensures the generation of stereochemically valid static models for complex, branched glycans. Predictions were performed using the locally installed AF3 source code on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. The top-ranked model (Rank 0) based on the pLDDT and PAE (Predicted Aligned Error) confidence scores was selected for subsequent energy analysis.  Quantitative Binding Energy Calculation with EvoEF2 To quantify the differences in binding affinity, we employed the EvoEF2 energy function, a physics-based scoring function optimized for computational protein design and binding energy estimation. (43) EvoEF2 has high accuracy and computational speed. This workflow provides the quantitative binding energy data requested, expanding on the energy minimization step. First, the PDB files generated by AlphaFold3 (Model 1 and Model 2) were pre-processed. We used EvoEF2 to calculate the resulting protein-protein interaction energy, Itotal, of the specific, glycan-induced conformation. This allowed us to isolate the energetic contribution of the glycan-mediated conformational stabilization on the protein-protein interface. Protein PDB files were first optimized using the RepairStructure command of EvoEF2. This step reconstructs incomplete side chains and optimizes the hydrogen-bonding network. Then, the binding energy between the IFN-β variant and the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor complex was calculated using the ComputeBinding command. The chains were split into two distinct interacting groups. Assuming IFN-β is chain A, IFNAR1 chain B, and IFNAR2 is chain C, the binding energy (∆Gbind) was computed as the difference between the total energy of the complex and those of the individual components (Chain A and Chain BC). The final Itotal value, which includes intra-chain van der Waals, electrostatic, hydrogen bonding, and solvation energy terms, is reported in kcal/mol. A more negative value indicates a more stable, higher-affinity interaction.
sampleProcessingProtocol: N-linked Glycan Profiling N-linked glycan profiles were analyzed using Ludger labeling kits (2-AB: LT-KAB-A2, Ludger, UK; procainamide: LT-KPROC-24, Ludger, UK). For protein denaturation and reduc-tion, 1 µL of 0.5 M dithiothreitol (DTT) (D5545; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and 10 µL of 1% RapiGest SF (186001861; Waters, USA) were added to 0.2 mg of buffer-exchanged protein. The mixture was incubated at 65°C in a heat block for 30 min. After reaction completion, 2 µL of PNGase F (P0705L; NEB, USA) was added for enzymatic deglycosylation. The reaction products were then purified using an EB10 Cartridge (LC-EB10-A6; Ludger, UK), and the eluted glycans were collected and dried in a centrifugal evaporator. The dried glycan samples were labeled with either 2-AB or procainamide, depending on the experimental requirements. N-linked glycan analysis was performed using a Thermo Ultimate 3000 system coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion™ Tribrid™ mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, MA, USA) with an elec-trospray ionization (ESI) source. Separation of labeled glycans was achieved using an AC-QUITY UPLC Glycan BEH Amide Column (2.1 × 150 mm2, 1.7 μm; Waters, USA). Chro-matographic separation was performed at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min, with a column temperature of 60°C for 2-AB–labeled glycans and 40°C for procainamide-labeled glycans. Fluorescence detection was performed at excitation and emission wavelengths of 310 and 370 nm, respec-tively. The mass spectrometer was operated under the following ESI conditions: a sheath gas flow rate of 50 Arb, an auxiliary gas flow rate of 10 Arb, an ion transfer tube temperature of 325°C, and a vaporizer temperature of 350°C. For MS/MS analysis, the Orbitrap detector was configured with a resolution of 120,000 and a scan range of 600–2,500 m/z. The top 15 pre-cursor ions with the highest intensities were selected for MS/MS. Precursor ions exceeding a minimum intensity threshold of 1.0 × 104 were considered strong and dynamically excluded for 7 s following their detection. Precursor ions with charge states of 1–3 were chosen for MS/MS fragmentation. For glycan fragmentation in higher-energy collision (HCD) mode, stepped collision energy percentages were adjusted based on precursor m/z values and charge states to ensure optimal fragmentation. Peptide Mapping To perform site-specific glycan analysis of R27T via peptide mapping, the protein was digested using chymotrypsin, trypsin, and Glu-C. The aim was to determine which enzyme provided optimal site-specific glycan characterization. Glycopeptides from each digestion were analyzed via LC-MS using a C18 column, with identification conducted through MS/MS analysis using Byos software and XICs generated from the MS spectra. For sample preparation, 1 mg of R27T was treated with a denaturing buffer [7 M guanidine-HCl and 0.25 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.4)] containing 5 mM DTT (D5545; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and incubated at 37°C for 60 min to fa-cilitate denaturation and reduction. Alkylation was performed by adding iodoacetamide (I4386; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) to a final concentration of 7.5 mM, followed by incubation in the dark at 25°C for 60 min. For enzymatic digestion, trypsin (11418025001; Roche, Switzerland) and chymotrypsin (11418467001; Roche, Switzerland) were added at a protein-to-enzyme ratio of 25:1 and incubated at 37°C for 18 h. Glu-C (11047817001; Roche, Switzerland) was used un-der the same ratio but incubated at 25°C for 18 h. Digested peptides were analyzed using the Thermo Ultimate 3000 system coupled to the Orbitrap Fusion™ Tribrid™ mass spectrometer with an ESI source (Thermo Scientific). Generated peptides were separated using an ACQUI-TY CSH C18 column (1.7 μm, 2.1 × 100 mm2; Waters, USA). MS analysis was conducted with the following parameters: a sheath gas flow of 50 Arb, an auxiliary gas flow of 10 Arb, an ion transfer temperature of 325°C, a vaporizer temperature of 350°C, spray voltage set to static, and a positive ion mode voltage of 3,500 V. MS/MS analysis was conducted using the Orbitrap detector with a resolution of 60,000, a scan range of 220–3,000, the RF lens set at 60%, an AGC target of 2.0 × 105, a maximum injection time of 50 ms, and microscans set to 1. Data analysis was conducted using Byos software (version 5.1.1; Protein Metrics Inc.) with a pre-cursor mass error tolerance of 20 ppm and a fragment mass error tolerance of 0.3 Da. Carbox-ymethylation was set as a common modification, whereas methionine oxidation and asparagine deamidation were considered rare modifications.

title: Disruption of Glucose Homeostasis in Prey: Combinatorial Use of Weaponized Mimetics of Somatostatin and Insulin by a Fish-Hunting Cone Snail
projectDescription: Venomous animals have evolved diverse molecular mechanisms to incapacitate prey and defend against predators. The majority of venom components characterized to date disrupt the nervous, locomotor, and cardiovascular system or causes tissue damage and degradation1. The discovery that certain species of fish-hunting cone snail use weaponized insulins to induce hypoglycemic shock in prey provided an unusual example for the use of toxins that target glucose homeostasis2. Here, we show that, in addition to insulins, the deadly fish hunter, Conus geographus, uses a selective agonist of the somatostatin receptor 2 (SSTR2) that potently blocks the release of the insulin-counteracting hormone glucagon, thereby exacerbating insulin-induced hypoglycemia in prey. The native toxin, Consomatin nG1, exists in several proteoforms that contain a minimized vertebrate somatostatin-like core motif connected to a heavily glycosylated N-terminal region. We demonstrate that the toxin’s N-terminal tail aligns with a glycosylated somatostatin peptide previously identified from fish pancreas and plays an important role in activating the fish SSTR2. Collectively, these findings provide a stunning example of chemical mimicry, highlight the combinatorial nature of venom components, and establish glucose homeostasis as an effective target for prey capture.
dataProcessingProtocol: Data analysis was performed using Preoteome Discoverer 2.5.0.400 (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.) for peak picking and Skyline 22.2.0.351 (ProteoWizard) for quality control and data integration.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Subfraction # 32, containing glycopeptides, was dried and reconstituted in 10 μL water. O-glycan release, labeling and C18 nanoLC-MS/MS analysis was performed as described previously with minor adjustments66. Briefly, an in-solution nonreductive O-glycan release was performed, using 15 μL 34% hydroxylamine and 29% 1,8-diazabicyclo(5.4.0)undec-7-ene (DBU) in water67 (75 min at 37 ºC). Released glycans were purified by 2 mg of magnetic hydrazide beads (MagSi-S Hydrazide beads 1 μm, magtivio B.V., Nuth), labeled using 2-aminobenzamide, and purified by cotton hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) using solid phase extraction (SPE)68 and further purified using porous graphitic carbon (PGC) SPE69. Prior to analysis the glycans were dried and reconstituted in 10 μL water. One μL per sample was separated by nanoflow liquid chromatograph using a single analytical column setup packed with Reprosil-Pure-AQ C18 phase (Dr. Maisch, 1.9 μm in particle size, 30 cm in column length) in an EASY-nLC 1200 UHPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using a PicoFrit Emitter (New Objectives, 75 μm in inner diameter). Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid (FA) in water, mobile phase B 0.1% FA in 80% ACN. A gradient from 2% to 38% mobile phase B in 20 min was used for elution of glycans. The emitter was interfaced to an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific) via a nanoSpray Flex ion source. A precursor MS scan (m/z 275-1700, positive polarity) was acquired in the Orbitrap at a nominal resolution of 120,000, followed by Orbitrap higher-energy C-trap dissociation (HCD)-MS/MS at a nominal resolution of 30,000 of the 10 most abundant precursors in the MS spectrum (charge states 1 to 4). A minimum MS signal threshold of 50,000 was used to trigger data-dependent fragmentation events. HCD was performed with an energy of 27 % ± 5 %, applying a 10 s dynamic exclusion window.

title: Binding of Akkermansia muciniphila to mucin is O-glycan specific
projectDescription: The intestinal anaerobic bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila is specialized in the degradation of mucins, which are heavily O-glycosylated proteins that constitute the major components of the mucus lining the intestine. Despite that adhesion to mucins is considered critical for the persistence of A. muciniphila in the human intestinal tract, our knowledge of how this intestinal symbiont recognizes and binds to mucins is still limited. Here, we first show that the mucin-binding properties of A. muciniphila are independent of environmental oxygen concentrations and not abolished by pasteurization. We then dissected the mucin-binding properties of pasteurized A. muciniphila by use of a recently developed cell-based mucin array that enables display of the tandem repeats of human mucins with distinct O-glycan patterns and structures. We found that A. muciniphila recognizes the unsialylated LacNAc (Galβ1-4GlcNAc1-R) disaccharide selectively on core2 and core3 O-glycans. This disaccharide epitope is abundantly found on human colonic mucins capped by sialic acids, and we demonstrated that endogenous A. muciniphila neuraminidase activity can uncover the epitope and promote binding. In summary, our study provides insights into the mucin-binding properties important for colonization of a key mucin-foraging bacterium.
dataProcessingProtocol: Structural annotation and relative quantification of the O-GalNAc glycans was performed as described before using the Minora Feature Detector node in Thermo Proteome Discoverer 2.2.0.388 (Thermo Fisher Scientific lnc.), GlycoWorkbench 2.1 (build 146 and the Thermo Xcalibur qual browser 3.0.63. Glycan structure annotation was based on literature and MS/MS analysis.
sampleProcessingProtocol: O-glycans on isolated secreted MUC2 reporters (WT and core3) and fetuin were released, derivatized, purified and analyzed by C18 nanoflow liquid chromatography (LC) coupled to mass spectrometry (MS) as described previously (de Haan et al. 2022; https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.1c05068). For each sample, 1 to 2 µg protein was mixed with 25 µL release reagent (20% hydroxylamine and 20% 1,8-diazabicyclo(5.4.0)undec-7-ene (DBU)) and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Released O-glycans were enriched by hydrazide beads and labeled with 50 µL 2-aminobenzamide (2-AB) reagent (500 mM 2-AB, 116 mM 2-methylpyridine borane complex (PB) in 45:45:10 methanol:water:acetic acid) for 2.5 h at 50 °C. Labeled glycans were purified by HILIC and porous graphitized carbon (PGC) SPE. Samples were resolved in 20 µL water for MS analysis.

title: C18  nanoLC-MS and Glycogenomics to Facilitate O-Glycan profiling in Human Cells
projectDescription: O-glycosylation is an abundant modification throughout the human proteome and plays a role in, amongst others, regulation of protein cleavage, protein folding, and modulation of cell-cell and -matrix interactions. O-glycosylation type and structure are important for biological function, demanding analytical methodologies that facilitate the annotation of O-glycans in biological material. While various successful strategies for the in-depth profiling of released O-glycans have been reported, these methods are often limitedly accessible to the non-specialist and/or challenged by the high abundance of O-glycan structural isomers. Here, we developed a high-throughput sample preparation approach for the non-reductive release of O-glycans from human cell material. Reducing-end labeling allowed efficient isomer separation and detection using C18 nano-liquid chromatography coupled to Orbitrap mass spectrometry (nanoLC-MS/MS). The implementation of glycogenetically engineered cell material proved a way into the complex structural annotation of O-glycan types and isomers. Using human keratinocytes as model system, we found a wide variety of O-glycan structures, including O-fucose, O-glucose, O-GlcNAc and O-GalNAc glycosylation, with the latter carrying both elongate Core 1 and Core 2 structures and varying numbers of fucoses and sialic acids. The method, including the now well characterized standards, provide the opportunity to study glycomic changes in human tissue and disease models using rather mainstream analytical equipment.
dataProcessingProtocol: MS1 feature detection in the raw files was performed using the Minora Feature Detector node in Thermo Proteome Discoverer 2.2.0.388 (Thermo Fisher Scientific lnc.). The [M+H] values of the resulting features were imported into GlycoWorkbench 2.1 (build 146) [17] and matched to glycan compositions with 0 to 8 hexoses, 0 to 8 N-acetyl hexosamines, 0 to 3 fucoses, 0 to 4 N-acetyl neuraminic acids and a 2-AB label. An additional matching was performed to glycan compositions with 0 to 6 hexoses, 0 to 6 N-acetyl hexosamines, 0 to 2 fucoses, 0 to 2 N-acetyl neuraminic acids, 0 to 3 pentoses and a 2-AB label. The complete list of identified compositions was imported into Skyline 21.1.0.146 (ProteoWizard), using the Molecule Interface.
